issues.legal_issue: A statement by a tenant’s brother claiming exclusive possession does not bind the tenant when the brother was not a party, agent, or person with a relevant interest.
material_facts: The eviction claim alleged that the tenant had sublet the premises to his brother.
The tenant was found to be the sole tenant and was not a party to the brother’s affidavit before the income tax authorities.
The brother claimed in the affidavit that he was the tenant in exclusive possession.
The brother was not the tenant’s agent and had no proprietary, pecuniary, or derivative interest in the premises.
issues.conclusion: The brother’s statement was inadmissible against the tenant and did not bind him.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 18 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872, statements are admissions when made by a party, an agent authorized expressly or impliedly by a party, a person with a proprietary or pecuniary interest in the subject matter while that interest continues, or a person from whom a party derived an interest while that interest continues. The brother’s statement did not fall within those categories. The issue arose in an eviction proceeding under Section 14(1)(b) of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958.

rule.if: eviction_case_alleging_subletting and statement_made_by_nonparty and speaker_lacked_authority and speaker_lacked_relevant_interest

predicates.eviction_case_alleging_subletting: The proceeding sought eviction on the ground that the tenant had sublet the premises.
predicates.statement_made_by_nonparty: A person who was not a party to the proceeding made a statement about possession of the premises.
predicates.speaker_lacked_authority: The person who made the statement was not authorized by the tenant to make it.
predicates.speaker_lacked_relevant_interest: The person who made the statement had no proprietary, pecuniary, or derivative interest in the premises.
predicates.nonparty_statement_does_not_bind_tenant: The nonparty’s statement does not bind the tenant.

issues.definition: When an eviction case alleges subletting and a nonparty’s statement is made without the tenant’s authority or a relevant interest, the statement does not bind the tenant.

issues.legal_issue: A court may re-examine and reappraise evidence underlying concurrent findings when those findings are primarily based on inadmissible evidence.
material_facts: The Rent Controller and the Rent Control Tribunal concurrently found that the tenant had sublet the premises, relying on the brother’s affidavit and oral evidence.
The affidavit was inadmissible against the tenant.
After excluding the affidavit, the High Court found no other evidence worth accepting to establish the brother’s exclusive possession and reappraised the oral evidence.
The High Court disbelieved the oral evidence and dismissed the eviction petition.
issues.conclusion: Once the finding of subletting was found to be vitiated because it was primarily based on inadmissible evidence, the High Court could re-examine and reappraise the evidence; the Supreme Court found no error in that reappraisal.
issues.legal_principle: In the context of an eviction claim under Section 14(1)(b) of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958, a finding primarily based on inadmissible evidence is vitiated in law. The court may re-examine and reappraise the remaining evidence. The inadmissibility of the brother’s statement was assessed under Section 18 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872. No earlier cases are relied on in the judgment.

predicates.review_of_concurrent_rent_findings: A court reviewing a rent-control decision considers concurrent findings on an eviction claim.
predicates.finding_based_primarily_on_inadmissible_: The finding under review rests primarily on evidence that is inadmissible against the party affected.
predicates.reappraisal_of_evidence_is_permissible: The reviewing court may re-examine and reappraise the evidence.

issues.definition: When a court reviews concurrent findings in a rent-control eviction matter and those findings rest primarily on inadmissible evidence, it may reappraise the evidence.

issues.legal_issue: A tenant’s operation of another business does not by itself establish that the tenant has surrendered exclusive possession or sublet the premises.
material_facts: The tenant was found to be the sole tenant of the premises.
The landlord argued that the tenant had another business and that this implied he was not in exclusive possession of the premises.
The Court found that having another business did not establish that the tenant lacked exclusive possession or had sublet the premises.
issues.conclusion: The tenant’s other business did not, by itself, establish that he lacked exclusive possession or had sublet the premises.
issues.legal_principle: In an eviction claim for subletting under Section 14(1)(b) of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958, the fact that a tenant has another business does not, without more, establish that the tenant has parted with possession or sublet the premises. No earlier cases are relied on in the judgment.

predicates.eviction_case_alleging_subletting: The proceeding sought eviction on the ground that the tenant had sublet the premises.
predicates.tenant_has_other_business: The tenant operates or has another business.
predicates.no_evidence_connects_other_business_to_t: No evidence connects the tenant’s other business to a transfer of possession of the premises.
predicates.other_business_alone_does_not_prove_subl: The tenant’s other business alone does not establish that the premises were sublet.

issues.definition: In an eviction case alleging subletting, if the tenant has another business but no evidence connects it to a transfer of possession, the other business alone does not prove subletting.
